# Deuteronomy 2 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

## v. 1: "Then we turned back and headed for the wilderness by way of the Red Sea… and for many days we wandered around Mount Seir."

- **Traditional reading (Gill):** After the rebellion at Kadesh, Israel obeyed God's command (Deut 1:40) and marched toward the Gulf of Aqaba. Gill thinks they came to Mount Seir near the close of the 38 years and "compassed" it for several days, not the whole 38 years. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** "Then" is simply "And" in Hebrew — no note of time. "By the way of the Red Sea" means southward toward the Gulf of Aqaba. "Many days" means "until near the close of the thirty-ninth year of the exodus." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic/evangelical):** Moses quickly advances to the end of the 38-year period; even under their unbelief and disobedience, God did not forsake Israel and still directed their journey. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **Precept Austin:** This departure is the *first* departure from Kadesh after the rebellion, not the second one recorded in Numbers 20:22. The "many days" are 38 years of wasted wilderness wandering. One writer calls this "the period of the anti-Exodus." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-2-commentary

## vv. 2–3: "At this time the LORD said to me, 'You have been wandering around this hill country long enough; turn to the north.'"

- **Gill:** God spoke while they were near Mount Seir. "Turn northward" — from Edom's southern border toward Canaan. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** This command was apparently issued when they were at Kadesh the second time, at the start of the 40th year (Numbers 20:1). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik:** "You have skirted this mountain long enough" — God directed Israel to advance northward toward the Promised Land. He also quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "He leads us by no unnecessary pathways. There are a meaning and a value in every stretch of the road, however rough and tortuous it may be." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **Precept Austin:** After 38 years of silence, God speaks again to Moses. The verb "turned" (*panah*) is the same word used for turning away from God spiritually. The idea: they physically turned toward the wilderness because spiritually their hearts had turned from God. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-2-commentary

## v. 4: "…pass through the territory of your brothers, the descendants of Esau… They will be afraid of you, so you must be very careful."

- **Gill:** They were not to pass through the *midst* of Edom but along its border. The Edomites feared that such a large host would seize their land. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** "Ye are passing through the border" — this was said before permission was requested from Edom (Numbers 20:17). Edom's fear was according to the prophecy of Exodus 15:15: "Then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Gray (concise):** Points out a seeming contradiction with Numbers 20:14 (where Edom refused passage and came out with a large army). The solution: in Numbers the Israelites were on Edom's western frontier where they were strong; now they were on the eastern side where Edomites were weaker. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/deuteronomy-2.html
- **Guzik:** The descendants of Esau (Edomites) were distant relatives through Jacob's brother Esau, 400 years earlier. God did not want Israel to take land He had given to Esau's descendants. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## v. 5: "Do not provoke them, for I will not give you any of their land, not even a footprint, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession."

- **Gill:** "Not so much as a foot breadth" — the sole of a man's foot. Jarchi noted a rabbinic interpretation that Israel would not receive Edom's land "until the day of the treading of the sole of the foot in the mount of Olives" (Zechariah 14:4), i.e., the Messianic age. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** It is noteworthy that the development of Ishmael preceded Isaac, and Esau's inheritance was won earlier than Jacob's. Isaac and Israel were still "strangers and sojourners" while the Edomites already had dukes and kings. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik:** Israel was probably strong enough to take Edom's land, but Israel only received what God had promised. They were not just another conquering army. Also quotes Thompson: "The divine commands were not uniformly instructions to go forward or to fight. Israel was to conquer some areas and by-pass others." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **Grant's Commentary (Brethren):** God had decreed that Edom was to have Seir; whoever fights against God's decrees will not prosper. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-2.html

## v. 6: "You are to pay them in silver for the food you eat and the water you drink."

- **Gill:** Though they had manna daily, they could buy other food when they had opportunity. They were not to take anything by force or stealth. Also notes that some rabbis read it as an interrogative ("Shall ye buy meat?" — no, there is no need), but Gill disagrees. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Spurgeon (via Guzik):** "Jarchi tells us that this exhortation meant that they were not to pretend to be poor… When the tribes came to the Edomites they were not to say to them, 'We are poor people, and have no money.' … Supplied by the infinite God, the children of heaven dare not pretend to be poor." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **Ellicott:** Compares to Genesis 14:23 ("Lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich") — God's people are not to be debtors or beggars among the nations. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Precept Austin:** "This is an amazing passage. Israel had been 38 years in the wilderness and yet God says they will have funds to purchase food and water. Amazing provision of God." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-2-commentary

## v. 7: "Indeed, the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands… These forty years the LORD your God has been with you; you have lacked nothing."

- **Gill:** God had increased their cattle and substance even in the wilderness. "These forty years" is a round number — the forty years were not yet fully complete. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** Suggests there is nothing unreasonable in the view that Israelites acquired wealth by trade or ordinary occupations during the wilderness journey. They had skilled workmen among them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Trapp (via Guzik):** "God, as a liberal Lord, gives not some small cottage or annuity, for life, to his elder servants, as great men use to do, but bountifully provides for them and theirs to many generations. Who would not serve thee then, O king of nations!" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **Precept Austin:** The Hebrew is literally "God has blessed you in all the work of your hands." This is an amazing statement given their disobedience at Kadesh. "If Yahweh had done this to rebels in the desert wanderings, would He do any less for them when they obeyed?" — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-2-commentary

## vv. 8–9: Israel passes by Edom and approaches Moab; God says, "Do not harass the Moabites… I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot."

- **Gill:** Elath and Ezion-geber were the two ports on the Red Sea in Edom. After Edom's refusal, Israel turned south to these ports, then northward, going around Edom to reach the wilderness of Moab. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** "The children of Lot, like those of Ishmael and Esau, had their earthly inheritance before the children of Abraham." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik:** The Moabites descended from Lot, Abraham's nephew. One of the more famous Moabites was Ruth (Ruth 1:4), who became great-grandmother to King David and an ancestor of the Messiah. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## vv. 10–12: Parenthetical note about the Emites, Rephaim, and Horites.

- **Gill:** The Emim were descendants of Ham, "a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims." They got their name from the fear and terror they put into people. The Horites (Horim) dwelt in caves in the rocks of Edom — the same people the Greeks called Troglodytae. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** These verses should be read parenthetically. The Emim, Zuzim, and Horim are first mentioned in Genesis 14:5–6. These tribes were flourishing in Abraham's time but were conquered before the exodus. The descendants of Esau "succeeded them" — a partial mixture of the two races produced the Amalekites (Genesis 36:12, 22). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik:** The term "giants" (*rephaim*) does not necessarily mean giants in stature but "fearsome ones." Clarke: "Probably they were a hardy, fierce, and terrible people, who lived, like the wandering Arabs, on the plunder of others." Thompson notes that *rephaim* in Psalm 88:10 and other places means "shades of the dead in Sheol" — possibly Israelites applied this term to long-dead early inhabitants. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **The phrase "just as Israel did"** (v. 12): Guzik cites Merrill, who says this may be a "perfective of confidence" — speaking of a future event as already done because God has promised it. Or it could be a later authorized addition. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## vv. 13–15: The Brook of Zered crossed; thirty-eight years from Kadesh-barnea; the generation of fighting men perished.

- **Gill:** "Zered" is both a valley and a brook. From Kadesh-barnea to Zered was exactly 38 years — all the generation numbered at Sinai (except Caleb and Joshua) had died. "The hand of the LORD was against them" refers to various judgments: the sword of Amalek, the plague at Shittim (24,000), Korah's rebellion (14,700), etc. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** The root *zârad* in Chaldee means "to prune." The name Zered suggests "willows of the brook," but Ellicott draws a spiritual analogy: it was the "valley of pruning" to the vine God brought out of Egypt — the last fruitless branches were removed here. Also notes that by the 40th year, the few remaining doomed men would have been "marked men" — everyone knew they had a short time to live. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik:** Thirty-eight years are covered in these brief verses. "This was a period when they didn't accomplish much more than survival, making little progress, and waiting for the generation of unbelief to die so that the generation of faith could enter the Promised Land." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## vv. 16–19: All the fighting men dead; God instructs Israel about Ammon: "Do not harass them… I have given it to the descendants of Lot."

- **Gill:** Ammon was not to be attacked because the Ammonites descended from Lot by his younger daughter (Genesis 19:38). Gill also notes that later half of Ammon's land was given to Gad — but that was land Sihon the Amorite had previously taken from Ammon, so Israel took it as Amorite territory, not Ammonite. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik:** "When all the men of war had finally perished" — this marked the end of the generation of unbelief. "Under the leadership of Moses, Israel was directed by God. They did not attack and conquer as they pleased, but as God directed." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## vv. 20–23: Parenthetical note about the Zamzummites, Horites, and Avvim/Caphtorites.

- **Gill:** The Zamzummim are thought to be the same as the Zuzim in Genesis 14:5. The name may mean "contrivers of evil and terrible things." The Avvim dwelt as far as Gaza; the Caphtorim (from Caphtor/Crete according to some) destroyed them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** The Caphtorim are the Philistines — compare Amos 9:7 ("the Philistines from Caphtor"). Some locate Caphtor in Cyprus or Crete. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik:** The point of these historical notes: if Edom, Moab, and Ammon could dispossess giant races, how much more could Israel dispossess the Canaanites under Jehovah's personal guidance. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## vv. 24–25: "Cross the Arnon Valley. See, I have delivered into your hand Sihon the Amorite… This very day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you upon all the nations."

- **Gill:** The Arnon was the border between Moab and the Amorites (Numbers 21:13). God had determined to give Sihon's land to Israel and here assures them of victory before battle. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** The territory from Arnon northward to Jabbok had been taken from Moab by the Amorites and was now to be possessed by Israel. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik:** This marks the transition — God would not let Israel take Edom, Moab, or Ammon, but He granted them the land of the Amorites (Sihon). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **JFB (Reformed influence):** At its mouth the Arnon is 82 feet wide and 4 deep, flowing between perpendicular sandstone cliffs. The whole country between Arnon and Jabbok had been seized by the Amorites, who were among the nations "doomed to destruction." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/deuteronomy-2.html

## vv. 26–29: Moses sends messengers of peace to Sihon, offering to pay for food and water, just as Edom and Moab had done.

- **Gill:** Messengers were sent from the Wilderness of Kedemoth (a city later belonging to Reuben). Moses used "words of peace" — a peaceable, respectful approach "to leave him inexcusable." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Ellicott:** By this peaceful message, Sihon was excepted from the catalogue of doomed nations according to the distinction drawn in Deuteronomy 20:10–11, 15–16. "He therefore brought his fate upon himself. He was offered the privileges of the Moabites whom he had conquered, and refused to accept the position." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm

## v. 30: "But Sihon… would not let us pass through, for the LORD your God had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate, that He might deliver him into your hand."

- **Gill:** (Covered in the long text — Gill simply narrates the refusal and the resulting battle.)
- **Ellicott — a careful, nuanced treatment:** "Jehovah gave the strength to Sihon, as He had done to Pharaoh, and as He does to all. Sihon was responsible for using the strength which God gave him in opposition to the Divine purposes. To 'harden' a man's spirit is not necessarily a moral process any more than the hardening of steel. 'Made obstinate' is the same verb used in Joshua 1:6 for 'Be of a good courage.' An unyielding spirit and a courageous heart are good or bad according to the use made of them. Sihon used them badly, Joshua used them well. God's gifts were the same to both." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic evangelical):** "It was right for God to do this because the Creator has the right to do whatever He pleases with His creatures. But it was also right because of the way God did it. God did not persuade a reluctant Sihon to act against Israel; God simply let Sihon's heart take the evil way it wanted to go. God did not change Sihon's heart from good to bad but hardened it in its malice towards Israel." Also quotes Thompson: "Both Pharaoh and Sihon were unaffected by the demands of God which came through God's servants. Neither would bend his will to the will of God and each refusal produced a further hardening of the heart." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **Grant's Commentary (Brethren):** God hardened Sihon's spirit with the object of delivering him into Israel's hand. The Amorite was not their brother as Esau was. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-2.html

## vv. 31–33: "The LORD said… See, I have begun to deliver Sihon… over to you." Battle at Jahaz; the LORD delivers Sihon into Israel's hand.

- **Gill:** The battle took place at Jahaz (or Jahazah), later a Levitical city in Reuben.
- **Ellicott:** "In all the conquests of Israel Jehovah gave the order to begin the attack." On v. 33, notes that "his sons" in the Hebrew is singular — "his son" (possibly a person of distinction).
- **Guzik:** God led Sihon into the destructive course his heart desired so the land of the Amorites became Israel's inheritance. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## vv. 34–35: "We captured all his cities and devoted to destruction the people of every city, including women and children… We carried off for ourselves only the livestock and the plunder."

- **Gill:** This was a war of *cherem* — complete devotion to destruction. Only livestock and material goods were taken as plunder.
- **Ellicott:** "Utterly destroyed" = devoted to destruction (*chêrem*), like the spoil of Jericho. "This could only be by Divine direction. The word implies nothing less. … the narrative asserts in this case an extermination of Sihon's people by the express command of Jehovah." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik:** This was "one of the unique wars of judgment God told Israel to fight." The Amorites were among the peoples God had long before appointed for judgment (Genesis 15:16) if they did not repent. Thompson: "It affirms the lordship of Yahweh over Israel and over his purposes for her in history, but also his judgment on wicked nations. … However, the application of the principle in the Christian age is very different." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## v. 36: "From Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley… even as far as Gilead, not one city had walls too high for us."

- **Guzik:** Thirty-eight years before, Israel refused to enter Canaan because they felt militarily over-matched (Deut 1:28 — "cities with walls up to heaven"). Here, walking in faith, "even high walls were obstacles that could be overcome in the strength of the LORD." The literal Hebrew is "there was not one city too *high* for us." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## v. 37: "But you did not go near the land of the Ammonites… or any place that the LORD our God had forbidden."

- **Gill:** Israel obeyed God's boundaries precisely.
- **Guzik:** Israel's conquests were not indiscriminate; they were bounded by God's specific commands. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### On the "hardening" of Sihon (v. 30):

- **Ellicott (Anglican/Exposition):** Softens the moral difficulty — hardening is like hardening steel, not necessarily moral. Sihon used God's gift of strength badly. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm
- **Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic):** Emphasises God's sovereign right as Creator; also stresses that God did not make Sihon evil but "let his heart take the evil way it wanted to go." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **Grant's (Brethren):** God hardened Sihon deliberately "with the object of delivering him into Israel's hand." A more direct sovereignty reading. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-2.html

### On the conquest and *cherem* (vv. 34–35):

- **Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic):** Notes this was a unique "war of judgment." Quotes Thompson that "the application of the principle in the Christian age is very different," implicitly distancing Christian practice from Holy War. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-2/
- **Ellicott:** Simply states the destruction was by "express command of Jehovah," leaving the moral question to the reader. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/2.htm

### On the land grants to Edom, Moab, and Ammon:

- **A recurring theme across traditions:** God as the sovereign disposer of all lands. Edom, Moab, and Ammon each received their territory by God's decree just as Israel would receive Canaan. Grant's (Brethren) commentary makes this explicit: "God had decreed that Edom was to have Seir… Whoever fights against this will not prosper." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-2.html

## What I Could Not Find

- **Lutheran-specific commentary** (1517.org or lcms.org) on Deuteronomy 2: no verse-by-verse material was discovered in the search results beyond Kretzmann's Popular Commentary excerpts, which mainly paraphrase the text without distinctive Lutheran doctrinal notes.
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings** (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org): the searches returned no results within the limits.
- **Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org): the searches returned no results.
- **Matthew Henry's full treatment** and the **Pulpit Commentary** full text could not be fetched due to limits, though Pulpit excerpts were available from the initial search — these largely align with Ellicott and Gill.
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / hyper-grace** readings of this chapter: no material from approved sources was found.

For the missing traditions, the chapter's themes (God's sovereignty over nations, holy war, the hardening of hearts) are treated very similarly across the available conservative Protestant commentaries, with the main difference being tone — some stress God's sovereign decree more directly, others emphasise human responsibility and the exceptional nature of the *cherem* commands.
